lawyer: Md Abul Hossain Khan, Advocate ------For the Petitioner.
parties:
Agrani Bank ----- Petitioner 
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat and others ----- Respondent
full_judgment:
2. Briefly stated, the facts are that the petitioner Bank instituted Money Suit No. 2 of 1993 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 1, Madaripur against the respondents for realisation of Taka 6,66,653/- The suit was decreed on contest on 13-6- 93 and the decretal amount stood at 7,48,361.82/- with cost.. The respondents paid a sum of Taka 1,75,000/- and there has been a balance of Taka 5,73,361.82/- for which the said Execution Case was started and after filing of the Execution Case respondent Nos. 2-9 paid a sum of Taka 4,82,073/- and there remained a balance of Taka 1,84,582 and including costs of the suit amounting to Taka 28,446.22/- the total amount came to Taka 2,13,029.12/-. Respondents No. 2-9 filed an application on 6-2-200 before the Artha Rin Adalat No.1 Madaripur to waive interest and the said Adalat in the absence of the learned Advocate of the petitioner Bank by an order dated 6-2-2000 waived the interest. The petitioner then filed an application under Order XLVII rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 24-4-2000 to review the said order which was rejected by the Artha Rin Adalat by impugned order dated 27-11-2002 with a finding that the review petition is not maintainable. 

 4. As regards the maintainability of the application under Order XLVII rule 1 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure the Artha Rin Adalat following the decision reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 196 maintained that the review petition is not entertainable. In Sultana Jute Mills Ltd and others vs Agrani Bank and others reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 196 = 46 DLR (AD) 174 it has been held that Revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division is provided for in section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and in making order under section 6 the proceeding, order, judgment and decree of an Artha Rin Adalat not amenable to interference by any court or authority, the aim of the Adalat Act was to create departures from the Code of Civil Procedure. Section 7, it may be said, was meant to be an exception to this complete ouster of interference. An exception has been made in respect of a judgment and decree in section 7(1). Another exception has been made in respect of a final order under Order IX rule 13 C.P.C. In both cases appeal will be to the High Court Division. There is room for argument that both the appellate and revisional powers of interference with any "order" interlocutory or otherwise, is expressly barred by section 6, the provision to section 7(1) barring an appeal against an interlocutory order has been provided for only as a measure of abundant caution. In other words, section 6 is the master ouster provision; section 7 is an exception to that ouster. The exception cannot render the ouster provision nugatory. There is scope for argument that if both appellate and revisional interlocutory orders of an Artha Rin Adalat are amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division, then section 6 is rendered largely nugatory. There was no need to say in section 6 that no "order" of an Artha Rin Adalat is amenable to interference by any Court or authority, when in the next breath all interlocutory orders, appellate and revisional, are supposedly made amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. There is also scope for further argument that revision is impliedly barred because the Adalat Act being a special legislation setting upon a special Court the remedies will follows as provided therein and if there is any exclusion indicated therein, as in section 6, it will include a remedy under the general law. Mr Md Abul Hossain Khan relying on this proposition has contended that since the-power of the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure is totally excluded in challenging this kind of interlocutory order the writ petition is maintainable. In paragraph 23 of the cited case it has been stated that our view is that in this case it matters little whether the High Court Division arrived at its decision on the counter-claim by way of revision or writ, because the counter-claim was not patently maintainable and there is nothing wrong in the finding of the High Court Division on this material question. 

 5. Therefore, we find that there was no clear indication that against an interlocutory order only the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution will lie. In paragraph 19 there is further indication that the court can exercise its inherent power under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The question again came before another Division Bench of this Court comprising Mr. Justice Mahmudul Amin Chowdhury and Mr. Justice Gour Gopal Saha in the case of Kazi Gowaherul Islam vs Standard Co-operative Society Ltd 50 DLR 333 and following the decision of Sultana Jute Mills Ltd case 1994 BLD (AD) 196 and it was observed that in deciding the validity of an interlocutory order under section 115(1) of the CPC the court is not left without power and the party is not left without relief. When it is apparent on the face of the record that the suit has been wrongly entertained and proceeded with in the Adalat, this Court may act under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure where it provided that nothing in this Code shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent power of the Court to make such order as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the court. The continuation of the suit before the Artha Rin Adalat is an abuse of the process of the Court as any decree passed by the Adalat in such a suit will be without jurisdiction and, as such, a nullity. As that has been filed under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure it is not maintainable against an order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, we are inclined to act under section 151 of the CPC Code and make that Rule absolute with a direction to the Adalat to return the plaint for presentation before the proper court. In the case of Islami Bank Bangladesh Limited vs AI- haj Md Shafiuddin Howlader and another reported in 2000 BLD (AD) 162 = 52 DLR (AD) 176 it has been held that Artha Rin Adalat has been set up under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 with a judicial officer as presiding officer for adjudication of claim of loan by the financial institutions which include banks. No special procedure has been provided for trial of ArthaRin suits under the said Ain. But to expedite disposal of those suits certain provisions have been made and power to file an application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and prefer appeal before the High Court Division have been given subject to deposit of half of the decretal dues. Under sub-section (4) of section 5 the Artha Rin Adalat is deemed to be a Civil Court and under sub-section (5) of section 5 Adalat is regulated by the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure unless there is anything contrary in the Ain. Ongoing through the provision of the Ain we do not find any provision therein which is contrary to the provision of Order IX rule 9 of the Code. Unless the order of disposal for default is allowed to be set aside the plaintiff bank would suffer loss and the borrower would be benefited. It is not the intention of the Ain to deprive a financial institution from realisation of its just dues from the borrower though there is sufficient reason for nonappearance of the plaintiff financial institution in Court on the date of hearing of the suit. From the absence of any provision in the Ain prohibiting filing of an application under Order IX rule 9 of the Code and from the specific mention of the Code in sub-section (5) of section 5 of the Ain we are of the view that provisions of Order IX rule 90f the Code may be followed by the plaintiff financial institution before the Artha Rin Adalat for setting aside an ex parte order of dismissal of the suit for default. 

 7. In the case of Sonali Bank vs Ali Tannery Ltd. and others Syed Amirul Islam, J sitting with Mr. Justice Gholam Rabbani considering the provision of Artha Rin Adalat Ain and various decisions of our jurisdiction and Indian jurisdiction has stated and observed that it had been held in a number of decisions that Artha Rin Adalat is not an ordinary Civil Court but a special forum of limited jurisdiction. The question therefore, arises where an order passed by a Court of special jurisdiction is revisable by this Court under section 115 CPC we can resolve this question easily if we can find an answer to the question, is the Artha Rin Adalat a Court Subordinate to the High Court Division. In deciding this issue with regard to special statutes the superior Courts of the subcontinent have formulated certain principles. If appeal lies from a special tribunal to the High Court then that special tribunal is subordinate to the High Court. Similarly, if the special Court is under the administrative control of the High Court, it is also subordinate to the High Court. If we examines the provisions of the Act we find that section 7 provides that an appeal shall lie against a judgment and decree of the Artha Rin Adalat to the High Court Division. Section 4(2) of the Act provides that the Judges of the Artha Rin Adalat will be appointed from amongst the Subordinate Judges in consultation with the Supreme Court. Rules framed under the Act provide that the Artha Rin Adalat will be under the administrative control of the Supreme Court. It has been held in one case that if the Court is one from which an appeal lies to the High Court though in certain specified cases, then the Court is subject to the appellate jurisdiction of the High Court and that is sufficient to attract the power of superintendence conferred on the High Court. Besides, Article 109 of the Constitution provides that High Court Division shall have superintendence and control over all courts subordinate to it and ultimately held that Artha Rin Adalat, though a special Court is nevertheless a Court, subordinate to the High Court Division and, is, therefore, amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court Division. So the revisional application is maintainable. 

 10. The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure so far as it relates to the procedure of holding trial of Artha Rin Adalat suit is applicable in the Artha Rin Adalat and the proceeding of the suit is regulated by some of the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure to make the suit ready for hearing, as for instance the issuance and service of summons after filing of the suit, the provision of substituted service, the amendment of the plaint, the provision of striking out or addition of parties under Order 1 rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the provision relating to production of documents under Rule 14 of Order XI, framing of issues, summons to the witnesses and attendance of the witnesses and all other provisions of like nature are applicable which are not in conflict with the Artha Rain Adalat Ain and the proceedings of Artha Rin suit are regulated by such provisions of the Code . After the finality of the proceeding i.e. after passing of the decree, the validity of the decree can be challenged in appeal in the manner as provided under section 7 of the Ain. After passing of the decree and in its execution proceedings, the same cannot be resisted by any third party or any party having interest in the property involved in the decree by resorting to the provisions of Order XXI and the rules thereunder as that would be contrary to the provision of the said Ain. In such a situation and in an appropriate case the third party's interest may be protected under general law as indicated in the Sultana Jute Mills case i.e. by taking recourse to filing a suit.
